question: Did Israeli parole judges really grant fewer paroles as their next meal break approached?
answer: Contested. A 2011 study found favourable rulings fell from about 65% to near zero across each session, then jumped after a break. Critics showed the order was not random: prisoners without lawyers tended to come last, and short cases were squeezed in before breaks. The hungry judges may have been tidy scheduling.
move: Before blaming tiredness for a pattern, check how the queue was ordered.
ask: When I see a pattern in my own bad days, have I checked what else was different about them?
reference: Weinshall-Margel & Shapard, Overlooked factors in the analysis of parole decisions, PNAS, 2011
